content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Across all four blind responses, peace is Hebrew shalom — comprehensive wholeness, well-being, and right relationship, centered on reconciliation with God accomplished through Christ ('peace with God'), and explicitly more than the absence of conflict. Complementary facets widely admitted: inner tranquility/freedom from anxiety (Phil 4:7), fruit of the Spirit, social peacemaking, holistic communal flourishing, and eschatological messianic peace. False peace (Jer 6:14) is noted as a counter-motif.","book_summary":"Peace is 'the covenant made whole' — shalom traced to a root meaning to complete, restore, repay; it is the work of righteousness and the great peace of those who love the law. The gospel publishes this restored covenant-peace. The book explicitly denies that peace is the world's truce or a feeling, and treats 'Peace, peace; when there is no peace' as the counterfeit: peace pronounced over an unkept covenant.","consensus_core_identification":"Peace = shalom-wholeness and right relationship with God (reconciliation through Christ), inclusive of inner tranquility, communal harmony, and eschatological restoration as complementary dimensions.","book_core_identification":"Peace = the covenant made whole — an objective covenantal state of restoration and completed obligation grounded in righteousness/law-keeping, published by the gospel; expressly not a truce and not a subjective feeling.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book excludes cases the consensus admits: inner tranquility/emotional calm (which every blind response lists as a common facet, citing Phil 4:6-7, Isa 26:3) is expressly ruled out ('not a feeling'), and mere cessation of conflict is ruled out as 'the world's truce.' The book also sharpens the false-peace motif from a peripheral counter-theme into a structural contrast: peace pronounced over an unkept covenant. Conversely, the book foregrounds a covenantal-legal condition (righteousness, love of the law) that the consensus does not make definitional.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"The book retains the consensus's central referent — shalom as restored wholeness/right relationship proclaimed in the gospel, with Eph 2:14 ('he is our peace') and John 14:27 shared across both. This is not a replacement of the referent, so DIVERGENT is inappropriate. But it is not a mere restatement: the book anchors peace specifically in covenant completion and the work of righteousness (Isa 32:17; Num 25:12; Ezek 34:25; 37:26), makes law-love a condition (Ps 119:165; Isa 48:18), and expressly rejects the subjective-tranquility dimension that the consensus treats as a legitimate complementary facet. That is a material tightening of boundary and conditions within the same category — REFINED with narrowing and reclassification of the 'inner feeling' cases out of the concept.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue MATCH: the consensus already defines peace as covenantal shalom-wholeness rather than absence of conflict, cites John 14:27 and Jer 6:14, and 'covenant made whole' could be read as just a compressed restatement of 'restored right relationship with God.' On that reading the exclusion of 'a feeling' merely echoes the consensus's own 'more than inner calm' caveat rather than genuinely rejecting the tranquility facet.","confidence":"medium"}
